content: Mononuclidic elements are chemical elements that possess either a single stable isotope or one very long-lived isotope that overwhelmingly dominates the element's natural isotopic abundance. There are 19 elements that fall into the first category, and three elements—bismuth (Bi), thorium (Th), and protactinium (Pa)—that belong to the second category. Elements such as rubidium (Rb), indium (In), and lanthanum (La), which have one stable isotope but also a significant fraction of a very long-lived isotope in their natural abundance, are not classified as mononuclidic. Mononuclidic elements are scientifically significant because their atomic weights can be measured with high precision. This is due to the minimal uncertainty associated with the isotopic abundances in a given sample, as these elements are dominated by a single isotope. Trace concentrations of unstable isotopes of some mononuclidic elements can be found in natural samples. For example, the isotope 53Mn, with a half-life of 3.7 million years, is produced through various cosmogenic and nuclear processes. Similarly, 137Cs, which has a half-life of 30 years, is generated through nuclear fission. These isotopes are utilized in a range of analytical and forensic applications. A complete list of mononuclidic elements and their isotopic compositions can be found in the publication Atomic Weights and Isotopic Compositions, edited by J. S. Coursey, D. J. Schwab, and R. A. Dragoset, published by the National Institute of Standards and Technology in 2005.
